text:
10 layers of AI. Most people know one.

Here is the full stack that powers ChatGPT.
Understanding the stack is the difference between using AI and actually building with it.

AI (Artificial Intelligence)
↳ The umbrella. Any technology doing tasks that normally require human intelligence.

ML (Machine Learning)
↳ How AI learns. From examples and data, not a list of rules. More data, better results.

Neural Networks
↳ Inspired by the human brain. Recognizes patterns and builds connections between them.

Deep Learning
↳ A deeper type of neural network. Multiple layers handling complex problems.

Transformers
↳ The breakthrough that made modern AI possible. Helps AI understand context and focus on what matters most.

GenAI (Generative AI)
↳ Where AI stops analyzing and starts creating. Text, images, code, video, music.

LLM (Large Language Model)
↳ Generative AI trained on language. Answers questions, explains ideas, holds conversations.

GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer)
↳ A specific type of LLM. The technology behind ChatGPT and most modern AI tools.

GPT-5.5
↳ One of the newest GPT models. Reasons better, solves harder problems, gives more accurate answers.

ChatGPT
↳ The product you open every day. GPT-5.5 is the engine. ChatGPT is the interface.


The biggest mistake leaders make is treating AI like software.
The real opportunity is treating it like a productivity multiplier.

Professionals who learn to work with AI will outperform everyone else. AI does not replace people. It amplifies them.

Save this. Someone in your network needs it.

♻️ Repost this to a leader still figuring out AI. peace :))

p.s. if your company is still debating whether to use AI, someone else already decided three layers ago ;)

text:
Every shelter I talk to says the same thing.

We need more donors.

I disagree.

Not because donors do not matter. 
Because most shelters already have people who care. 
They just have no system for keeping them.

I have looked at donation data from shelters across Canada and the US and the pattern is almost identical everywhere.

→ Donor gives once 
→ Gets a generic thank-you 
→ Never hears a personal word again until the next campaign asks for money

That is not a fundraising strategy. 
That is a leaky bucket.

You keep pouring new donors in from the top while the existing ones quietly walk out the bottom.

The donors are not gone. They just stopped feeling like they were part of something.

And fixing that, the emails, the updates, the individual animal stories, would do more for most shelters than any new campaign ever could.

The solution is not more donors.

It is a better conversation with the ones you already have.

I put together a free playbook on exactly how to do that.

Comment "DONORS"
and I will send it over.

text:
That rescue dog sitting quietly in the corner is not ignoring you.

You are just reading the wrong signals.

Rescue dogs do not show trust the way people expect. 

No running to you on day three. 
No cuddling on command. 

Trust looks a lot quieter than that, and most new adopters miss it completely.

Here is what it actually looks like.
→ Sleeping near you instead of the far corner. That is a choice.
→ Yawning around you. In dog behavior, yawning signals comfort, not boredom.
→ Following you between rooms without whining. That is attachment, not anxiety.
→ Showing you their belly. One of the most vulnerable things a dog can do.
→ Bringing you something. A toy, a sock, anything. That is an invitation.
→ Brief eye contact, then looking away. Not a stare. A check-in.

Most of these happen in the first 30 days and go completely unnoticed.

If your rescue dog is doing even two or three of these, they are not indifferent.

They are just taking their time.

I put together a free checklist of settling-in signals for the first 90 days with a rescue dog.

Comment "TRUST"
and I will send it your way.

text:
Repeat donations doubled in 90 days.

She did not run a new campaign. 
She rewrote one sentence in her thank-you email.

Here is what she changed.
After "thank you for your donation," she added the name of the animal the donor helped, one thing that animal did that week, and then this question at the bottom.

"Would you like us to update you when there is news about him?"
Donors who said yes started opening every email.

Some of them replied. 
Some of them gave again without being asked, just because they wanted to know what happened to the dog.

I have been thinking about this since she told me. 
Most shelter thank-you emails are basically receipts. 
Amount, date, tax ID. Sent and forgotten.

But the thank-you email arrives at the exact moment a donor feels most connected to your cause. 
What you do with that moment determines whether they give once or give for years.

She figured that out. And it cost her nothing to change.

I put the exact email structure she used into a free playbook, along with a few others built the same way.

Comment "PLAYBOOK"

Before I built BarkLogue, 
I spent six months reading every study I could find on why people donate to animal causes.

47 papers.

One finding appeared in almost all of them.

It is called the identifiable victim effect.

People donate significantly more to one named, individual animal than they do to statistics about thousands of animals.

The more specific and individual the story, the more people give.

The more abstract and aggregate the appeal, the less they give.

This is not a theory.

It has been replicated across dozens of studies in multiple countries.

And yet the majority of shelter fundraising is built entirely on aggregate appeals.

"Thousands of animals need your help."

"Every year, millions of dogs are surrendered."

These statements are true.

They are also, according to the research, among the least effective ways to ask for donations.

What works is a name.

A detail.

A personality.

Something that makes one animal real to one person who then feels like they specifically can help.

That is what BarkLogue gives every animal in a shelter.

I put together a one-page summary of the most important research on donor psychology in animal welfare.

Practical, plain language, useful for anyone running fundraising appeals.

Comment "RESEARCH" and I will send it over.

text:
Are you killing your dog? 
Unknowingly..

There are five foods in most kitchens right now that can kill a dog in under 24 hours.

Two of them are considered healthy for humans.

Most pet owners know about chocolate.

Fewer know about the others.


❗️Grapes and raisins.
The exact toxic dose is still unknown, which means there is no safe amount.

Kidney failure can begin within 24 hours. 

Even a small handful has killed dogs.


❗️Xylitol.
This is in sugar-free gum, some peanut butters, toothpaste, and a growing number of baked goods.

In dogs it triggers a rapid insulin release and can cause liver failure.

Check the ingredient list on anything sugar-free before it goes near your dog.


❗️Onions and garlic.
Both destroy red blood cells in dogs.

Cooked, raw, powdered. All of it.


❗️Macadamia nuts.
Not fatal in most cases but cause vomiting, tremors, and high fever within 12 hours.


❗️Cooked bones.
They splinter into sharp pieces that can perforate the stomach lining.

If your dog eats any of these, call your vet immediately.


Do not wait for symptoms.

text:
Most dogs will not tell you when they are in pain.

Not because they are hiding it.

Because they are wired not to show weakness.

By the time a dog is limping or crying, the pain has usually been there for a while.

Vets use a simple observation to catch it earlier.

Most pet owners have never heard of it.

Here is what to look for when your dog is resting and not expecting attention.

Squinting or partially closed eyes when nothing is in them.

Tension around the muzzle or jaw.

Ears pulled back flat rather than relaxed to the side.

Whisker and cheek tension that changes the shape of the face.

A hunched or sunken posture even when lying down.

None of these alone means something is wrong.

But two or three together, consistently, is worth a vet conversation.

This matters especially for rescue animals.

Shelter dogs have often learned to hide pain as a survival behavior.

A dog that looks completely fine during an adoption meeting may have been managing discomfort for months.

I put together a free checklist of what to watch for in the first 90 days with a rescue animal.

Lock positioning before touching Figma

text:
MIT researchers found why AI fails on long documents.

Even when the file fits inside the context window.

You paste a 200-page PDF.
Ask a simple question.

AI answers wrong.

Even though the correct line sits in the document.

This problem is called Context Rot.

→ More context can reduce accuracy
→ Models lose recall and reasoning
→ Not because of limits
→ Because too much information arrives at once

The solution: Recursive Language Models (RLMs).

Instead of giving the model the entire document, it explores the context step by step.

→ Peek small sections
→ Search keywords
→ Filter relevant parts
→ Solve smaller pieces recursively

Think of it like this.

Parent model asks the question.
Child models solve smaller tasks.
The parent combines the results.

The insight is simple.

Traditional LLMs:
“Here is everything. Figure it out.”

RLMs:
“Here are tools. Explore the data.”

This is the same idea behind modern AI agents and coding assistants.

Accuracy does not derive from a larger context.

It comes from better context navigation.

I will share the research paper.

This is the best way to automate these days:

n8n Error Workflow + Claude Code (MCP) = auto-fix loop

How it works behind the scenes:
1. Your main n8n workflow fails

3. It sends the workflow ID + failed node + error message to Claude Code

→ wrong data types (array vs item)

But it won’t magically solve everything.

Some failures still need you:

→ expired credentials

text:
Everyone talks about LLMs, but there's a whole family of specialized models doing incredible things.

8 AI model architectures, visually explained:

1. LLM (Large Language Models)
→ Text goes in, gets tokenized into embeddings, processed through transformers, and text comes out.

↳ ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.


2. LCM (Large Concept Models)
→ Works at concept level, not tokens. Input is segmented into sentences, passed through SONAR embeddings, then uses diffusion before output.

↳ Meta's LCM is the pioneer.


3. LAM (Large Action Models)
→ Turns intent into action. 
→ Input flows through perception, intent recognition, task breakdown, then action planning with memory before executing.

↳ Rabbit R1, Microsoft UFO, Claude Computer Use.


4. MoE (Mixture of Experts)
→ A router decides which specialized "experts" handle your query. Only relevant experts activate, results through selection and processing.

↳ Mixtral, GPT-4, DeepSeek.


5. VLM (Vision-Language Models)
→ Images pass through a vision encoder, text through a text encoder. Both fuse in a multimodal processor, then a language model generates output.

↳ GPT-4V, Gemini Pro Vision, LLaVA.


6. SLM (Small Language Models)
→ LLMs optimized for edge devices. Compact tokenization, efficient transformers, quantization for local deployment.

↳ Phi-3, Gemma, Mistral 7B, Llama 3.2 1B.


7. MLM (Masked Language Models)
→ Tokens get masked, converted to embeddings, then processed bidirectionally to predict hidden words.

↳ BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa power search and sentiment analysis.


8. SAM (Segment Anything Models)
→ Prompts and images go through separate encoders, feed into a mask decoder to produce pixel-perfect segmentation.

↳ Meta's SAM powers photo editing, medical imaging, and autonomous vehicles.

text:
Your AI Agent is “wrong”… But let me be honest.
90% of the time, it’s not the model.

It’s the data you showed it.

(i'm sharing my own decison template i use worth $47 for free).

Most people make this mistake.

Agent gives unexpected answers
→ you instantly add a Vector DB
→ Sounds smart.
→ Feels advanced.
→ And sometimes… it actually makes things worse.

—

but, here’s the hard-truth (most people are going to hate me).

The fix is not more tools.
The fix is choosing the right retrieval method.
That’s RAG.

Before building anything, pause and ask:

→ What questions will users actually ask?
→ What context does the agent really need to answer correctly?

That’s Context Engineering.

And this part decides whether your agent feels smart
or a confident stupid. (lol!)

—

Here’s a simple 5-second decision rule I use:
1. Filters (fastest + cheapest)
→ If a human would filter in Excel, use filters
↳ product, date, status, quantity

2. SQL (best for math + rankings)
→ If a human would use pivot tables, use SQL
↳ totals, trends, top 3, averages

3. Full Context (best for order + accuracy)
→ If a human would read the entire document, use full context
↳ timelines, processes, summaries

4. Vector Search (best for “find the right part”)
→ If you need semantic search across large text, use embeddings
↳ huge knowledge bases, “where is this mentioned?”

Why vector search fails with numbers:
→ It may retrieve only one chunk
→ Your agent answers from partial rows
→ “Highest sales week” becomes a confident wrong guess

—

The real goal is simple → Pull only what’s needed.

↳ cheaper tokens
↳ fewer hallucinations
↳ better answers

Even on GPT-5. (or upcoming newer)

15 AI Skills to Master for 2026

AI is no longer just a tool you use.

It’s a skillset you build.

Here’s a clear, practical list of the most important AI skills to focus on, and what each one actually means.


-


1. Prompt Engineering
Knowing how to clearly instruct AI using structure, constraints, and intent so outputs are accurate, useful, and consistent.

2. Multimodal AI
Working with AI that understands text, images, audio, and video together, enabling richer analysis and more human-like creation.

3. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Connecting AI to documents, databases, and private knowledge so answers are grounded in real, trusted data.
 
4. AI Agents
Building autonomous systems that can plan, decide, and execute multi-step tasks with minimal human input.

5. AI Workflow Automation
Using AI + automation tools to eliminate repetitive work by connecting apps, data, and decision logic.

6. AI Tool Stacking
Combining multiple AI and productivity tools into one system instead of relying on a single platform.

7. Fine-Tuning & AI Assistants
Customizing AI behavior or building assistants that match a specific domain, tone, or business workflow.

8. LLM Management
Monitoring AI performance in production, tracking accuracy, hallucinations, latency, and cost.

9. AI Chatbots
Designing conversational systems for support, onboarding, sales, and internal knowledge access.

10. AI Content Marketing
Using AI to research, write, optimize, and scale content that educates, ranks, and converts.

11. AI Video Creation
Turning scripts or ideas into videos using AI for editing, visuals, and motion, without full production teams.

12. Voice AI & Avatars
Generating realistic voices and digital presenters for training, education, sales, and assistants.

13. Website Creation with AI
Building fast, professional websites using AI-powered no-code and low-code platforms.

14. AI SaaS Development
Shipping lightweight AI products, tools, and prototypes quickly to test ideas or launch startups.

15. Staying Updated in AI
Continuously tracking new models, tools, and shifts in the ecosystem to stay relevant in a fast-moving field.


-


You don’t need to master all 15 at once.

But in 2026, the people who understand how these skills connect will outpace those who only know individual tools.

Learn these 17 nodes to tackle 80% n8n errors.

That’s not an opinion.
That’s how we actually build for clients.

You need these practical ones 👇

If you master just these, you can build 80% of real client workflows.

1. Manual Trigger
Used for testing and debugging workflows before going live.

2. Schedule Trigger
Run automations daily, weekly, or at fixed times (works while you sleep).

3. App / Event Trigger
Starts workflows from Gmail, Slack, forms, CRMs, payments, etc.

4. Webhook
Receive data from websites, tools, or custom apps instantly.

5. Respond to Webhook
Send results back to the app or frontend after processing.

6. Set (Edit Fields)
Clean, rename, structure, and control data flowing through your workflow.

7. Split Out
Break lists into individual items so actions run one by one.

8. Aggregate
Bring multiple items back into a single structured output.

9. Loop Over Items
Process large datasets safely without rate limits or crashes.

10. IF
Basic decision-making logic (true / false paths).

11. Switch
Route data into multiple paths based on conditions or categories.

12. Merge
Combine outputs from different branches into one flow.

13. HTTP Request
Connect to any API, even if n8n has no native integration.

14. Code
Handle predictable data logic faster and cheaper than AI.

15. AI Node (LLM)
Generate, summarize, classify, or rewrite content.

16. AI Agent
Let AI think, remember, decide, and use tools automatically.

17 Agent Tools
Give agents power to send emails, call APIs, update databases.

18. Google Sheets
Store, read, and manage data easily (the automation workhorse).

text:
You can keep yelling at GPT.
Or you can give it a real job description.

When I work with advanced models, I treat every prompt like a mini-spec.
5 layers, always in the same order.

Here is how that looks in practice.

1) PURPOSE
"Help me design a decision tree for qualifying inbound leads."

2) ROLE
"You are a senior RevOps manager in a B2B SaaS company."

3) INSTRUCTIONS
"Ask up to 5 clarifying questions first.
Then propose the decision tree.
Return it as a simple text outline I can paste into n8n."

4) MANNER
"Direct. Structured. No marketing language."

5) EFFORT
"Reason step by step.
Consider edge cases like missing data or duplicate leads."

This is the same pattern I plug into:
- AI agents that run 24/7
- Automation flows that touch CRM, email, Slack
- Any prompt where "close enough" is not good enough

If one of these layers is missing, quality drops.
If PURPOSE or ROLE is missing, quality crashes.

Next time you are about to type a one-line request into GPT, pause.

Then judge the model by the answer.

text:
Most people don’t realize this… n8n used classic design patterns in their User-Experience.

.. and it's exactly why It outperformed Zapier and Make.

Even if you’ve never studied them.

Here are the only ones that actually matter:
1. Adapter → When you clean or reshape API data (Set / Function / Transform).

2. Observer → Triggers (webhooks, schedules, emails).

3. Factory → Creating tasks, leads, or JSON objects based on inputs.

4. Command → Call Workflow = reusable, packaged logic.

5. Facade → Hide 10 messy steps inside one clean sub-workflow.

6. Composite → Parent workflow → child workflows → shared logic.

7. Template Method → Same workflow structure, small variations.

8. Flyweight → Reuse credentials, env variables, static data.

9. State → Branching based on status, flags, or conditions.


Why it helps beginners:
✓ Less duplication. 
✓ Cleaner structure. 
✓ Easier debugging. 
✓ Scales to more clients.

text:
How to Use Nano Banana Pro Inside n8n 
(Short, Clear Steps)
Grab the workflow and the Notion file.


1. Get access + API key

2. Set up a simple n8n workflow

3. Make your request to Nano Banana Pro

→ This first call gives you a task ID, which basically means,
“Your image is being prepared. Hold on.”

(Exact body format is inside the Notion file.)


4. Poll until the image is finished
→ n8n checks every few seconds to see if the image is ready.
→ If it’s still generating → wait and check again.
→ If it fails → stop.
→ If it succeeds → move forward.

This loop continues until Nano Banana Pro says:
“Your image is done.”


5. Get the final image URL
Once the task finishes, you get a public image link.
You can now:
→ Save it to Google Drive
→ Send it via WhatsApp or email
→ Add to Notion
→ Use it in another automation

n8n handles all of this automatically.

AI that can actually do multi-step work on a computer: think, use tools, think again, take actions, check results, keep going.

What it can do (live demos we ran):

1. Plan and book a full wedding weekend (travel, outfit, gift, logistics).
2. Analyze a messy data export → build a clean deck for work.
3. Coordinate real-world tasks across multiple apps/accounts.

Why this matters: Until now, most AI has given you answers. Agent gives you execution. It combines the spirit of Deep Research + digital Operator…but goes further because it can reason, act, re-check, and iterate.

Allowing it to think and act, proactively choosing from a toolbox of agentic skills to complete tasks for you using its own computer.

However, this does pose some major risks...

Sam Altman said this "We don’t know exactly what the impacts are going to be, but bad actors may try to “trick” users’ AI agents into giving private information they shouldn’t and take actions they shouldn’t, in ways we can’t predict. We recommend giving agents the minimum access required to complete a task to reduce privacy and security risks.

For example, I can give Agent access to my calendar to find a time that works for a group dinner. But I don’t need to give it any access if I’m just asking it to buy me some clothes.

There is more risk in tasks like "Look at my emails that came in overnight and do whatever you need to do to address them, don’t ask any follow up questions”. This could lead to untrusted content from a malicious email tricking the model into leaking your data."

The risk mitigation strategy will continue to evolve.

text:
YouTube is cracking down on “AI slop.”

Not all AI use is banned.

But spammy, mass-produced videos?

Those are in serious trouble.

Starting July 15, 2025 —
YouTube’s Partner Program will tighten rules on what kind of content can be monetized.

Here’s what’s changing:

• Repetitive, templated content made using AI tools won’t earn revenue.
• Automated slideshows, AI voiceovers, or reused clips = risk of demonetization.
• Creators using AI responsibly to add original value? You're still safe.
• No change for high-quality AI-enhanced content — only for low-effort spam.

This is not a new rule —
YouTube has long disapproved such content.

However, enforcement is now becoming stricter.

So if your strategy relies on low-effort automation —
You have until July 15 to pivot.

YouTube isn’t anti-AI.
It’s anti-noise.

Will your content survive the clean-up?

#YouTubeUpdate #CreatorEconomy #AIContent #Monetization
